label: lem:reflected:timechange
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:reflected:timechange}
Under Assumption~\ref{asmpt:continuous:regularity}, the normally reflected martingale problem with Neumann boundary condition for
$$
\mathcal Lf=e^{U-U_0}\bigl(\Delta f-\langle\nabla U_0,\nabla f\rangle\bigr)
$$
is well posed for every initial point in $\mathcal C$. Write $(P_t)_{t\geq0}$ for its transition semigroup.

label: prop:continuous:structure
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:continuous:structure}
Under Assumption~\ref{asmpt:continuous:regularity}, let $(P_t)_{t\geq0}$ be the transition semigroup from Lemma~\ref{lem:reflected:timechange}, and write $Z:=\int_{\mathcal C}e^{-U(x)}dx$ and $\pi(dx):=Z^{-1}e^{-U(x)}\mathbf1_{\mathcal C}(x)dx$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item For $f\in C^2(\overline{\mathcal C})$ satisfying the Neumann condition
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:boundary}
\nabla f\cdot\nu=0\quad\text{on }\partial\mathcal C,
\end{equation}
the generator acts as
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:generator}
\mathcal Lf=e^{U-U_0}\bigl(\Delta f-\langle\nabla U_0,\nabla f\rangle\bigr).
\end{equation}
\item The form
$$
\mathcal E(f,g):=\frac1Z\int_{\mathcal C}e^{-U_0(x)}\langle\nabla f(x),\nabla g(x)\rangle dx,\qquad \mathcal D(\mathcal E)=H^1(\mathcal C),
$$
is a densely defined closed symmetric Markov form on $L^2(\pi)$ whose semigroup is $P_t$. Its nonpositive self adjoint generator agrees with $\mathcal L$ on the Neumann test functions in (i). Moreover, $P_t1=1$ and, for every $f\in L^2(\pi)$ and $t>0$,
$$
P_tf\in\mathcal D(\mathcal L),\qquad
\frac{d}{dt}\|P_tf\|_{L^2(\pi)}^2=-2\mathcal E(P_tf,P_tf).
$$
\item The semigroup $P_t$ admits a jointly continuous, strictly positive Neumann heat kernel $\kappa_t(x,y)$ relative to $\pi$ on $(0,\infty)\times\mathcal C\times\mathcal C$, including boundary points. The Lebesgue transition density $p(t,x,y)=\kappa_t(x,y)Z^{-1}e^{-U(y)}$ has the same continuity and positivity properties. In particular, for every $s>0$,
$$
0<\min_{x,y\in\mathcal C}\kappa_s(x,y)\leq\max_{x,y\in\mathcal C}\kappa_s(x,y)<\infty.
$$
\end{enumerate}

body_md:
\label{thm:chi:square}
Under Assumption~\ref{asmpt:continuous:regularity}, assume that $\mu_0\ll\pi$ and $\chi^2(\mu_0\Vert\pi)<\infty$. If $\pi$ satisfies the Poincar\'{e} inequality
$$
    \operatorname{Var}_{\pi}(f)
    \leq
    C_P\int_{\mathcal C}\|\nabla f\|^2\,d\pi
$$
for every $f\in H^1(\mathcal C)$, \footnote{This is the standard spectral gap form of the Poincar\'e inequality. See e.g. \cite{Bakry2008,Bakry2013}.}then
\begin{equation}
	\chi^{2}(\mu_{t}\Vert\pi)\leq
	\chi^{2}(\mu_{0}\Vert\pi)e^{-2\alpha_{0} t/C_{P}},
\end{equation}
provided that $\alpha_{0}:=e^{\inf_{x\in\mathcal{C}}(U(x)-U_{0}(x))}>0$.

\label{cor:complexity}
Under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:final}, fix $\varepsilon>0$ and set
$$

\begin{equation}\label{eq:complexity:valid:k}
    k\geq\max\{3,T_\varepsilon\},

    \frac{k}{(\log k)^2}
    \geq
    \frac{16\bar C_0^4T_\varepsilon^3}{\varepsilon^4},

$$

$$

    =\widetilde{\mathcal O}\left(
    T_\varepsilon+\frac{\bar C_0^4T_\varepsilon^3}{\varepsilon^4}

\begin{align}\label{under:additional}

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{(i)} For a Neumann test function $f$, Lemma~\ref{lem:reflected:timechange} gives
$$
\frac{P_tf(x)-f(x)}{t}=\frac1t\mathbb E^x\left[\int_0^t\mathcal Lf(X_s)\,ds\right]\rightarrow\mathcal Lf(x).
$$
The limit follows from continuity of the paths and bounded continuity of $\mathcal Lf$, proving~\eqref{eqn:generator}.

\emph{(ii)} Set $w=Z^{-1}e^{-U}$ and $q=Z^{-1}e^{-U_0}$. Continuity and compactness give constants $0<c_-\leq c_+<\infty$ bounding both weights. Hence,
$$
\begin{aligned}
c_-\|f\|_{H^1(\mathcal C)}^2 &\leq\|f\|_{L^2(\pi)}^2+\mathcal E(f,f)=\int_{\mathcal C}\left(|f|^2w+\|\nabla f\|^2q\right)\,dx
\leq c_+\|f\|_{H^1(\mathcal C)}^2.
\end{aligned}
$$
Completeness and density of $H^1(\mathcal C)$ therefore make $\mathcal E$ closed and densely defined on $L^2(\pi)$.  
For the truncation $\Phi(r)=\min\{1,\max\{0,r\}\}$, the Sobolev chain rule gives $|\nabla\Phi(f)|\leq|\nabla f|$ almost everywhere, so $\mathcal E(\Phi(f),\Phi(f))\leq\mathcal E(f,f)$, which is the Markov property. Smooth restrictions are dense in $H^1(\mathcal C)$ by the extension property of the domain, and dense in $C(\mathcal C)$ in the uniform norm, giving regularity. If $f$ is constant on a neighborhood of the support of $g$, the gradient integral defining $\mathcal E(f,g)$ vanishes, giving strong locality.

Let $\mathsf A\geq0$ be the associated self adjoint operator and $S_t=e^{-t\mathsf A}$. For a Neumann test function $f$ and $g\in H^1(\mathcal C)$, integration by parts gives
$$
\mathcal E(f,g)=-\frac1Z\int_{\mathcal C}g\,\nabla\cdot\left(e^{-U_0}\nabla f\right)\,dx
=-\langle\mathcal Lf,g\rangle_{L^2(\pi)}.
$$
Thus $-\mathsf Af=\mathcal Lf$ and $\mathsf A1=0$. The associated conservative diffusion solves the Neumann martingale problem for $\pi$ almost every initial point by \cite[Theorems~7.2.1, 7.2.2 and~5.2.2, Eq.~(5.2.26)]{FOT2011}, using boundedness and a countable dense family of Neumann tests in the norm $\|f\|_\infty+\|\mathcal Lf\|_\infty$. Uniqueness in Lemma~\ref{lem:reflected:timechange} identifies $S_t=P_t$ on $L^2(\pi)$. Hence $P_t1=1$, and spectral calculus gives $P_tf\in\mathcal D(\mathsf A)$ for $t>0$ and
$$
\frac{d}{dt}\|P_tf\|_{L^2(\pi)}^2
=-2\langle P_tf,\mathsf AP_tf\rangle_{L^2(\pi)} =-2\mathcal E(P_tf,P_tf).
$$

\emph{(iii)} On the closed convex state space $\mathcal C$, the unweighted Neumann form has the complete Euclidean intrinsic metric. Convexity gives volume doubling and the Poincar\'e inequality on $D_r=\mathcal C\cap B(x,r)$,
$$
\begin{gathered}
|D_{2r}|\leq2^d|D_r|,\quad f_{D_r}:=\frac1{|D_r|}\int_{D_r}f\,dx, \quad \int_{D_r}|f-f_{D_r}|^2dx\leq c_dr^2\int_{D_r}\|\nabla f\|^2dx.
\end{gathered}
$$
The bounds on $w,q$ make the weighted measure and form uniformly comparable to the unweighted ones, and their intrinsic metrics equivalent. Thus \cite[Theorem~3.5 and Corollary~3.6]{sturm1996localIII} gives the parabolic Harnack inequality, and \cite[Proposition~3.1, Theorems~4.1 and~4.8]{sturm1996localIII} gives a jointly continuous, strictly positive kernel $\kappa_t(x,y)$ on $(0,\infty)\times\mathcal C^2$, including the boundary. 

To justify continuity in the initial point, couple the base diffusions $Y^{x_n}$ and $Y^x$ with the same Brownian motion, where $x_n\to x$. Additive noise cancels in their difference, and the convex reflection sign gives
$$
\sup_{0\leq u\leq T}\left\|Y_u^{x_n}-Y_u^x\right\|\leq e^{\operatorname{Lip}(\nabla U_0)T}\|x_n-x\|.
$$
Since $a^{-1}$ is uniformly continuous on $\mathcal C$, the clocks $A_u^{x_n}=\int_0^u a(Y_r^{x_n})^{-1}dr$ converge uniformly to $A_u^x$ on bounded intervals. Their slopes lie between $1/a^*$ and $1/a_*$, so their inverse clocks also converge uniformly on bounded intervals. Continuity of the base paths now gives $X_t^{x_n}=Y^{x_n}_{\tau_t^{x_n}}\to Y^x_{\tau_t^x}=X_t^x$ almost surely. For bounded continuous $f$, dominated convergence yields $P_tf(x_n)\to P_tf(x)$, proving the Feller property.
For $f\in C(\mathcal C)$, the identity $P_tf(x)=\int_{\mathcal C}\kappa_t(x,y)f(y)\pi(dy)$ from part~(ii) therefore extends from $\pi$ almost every $x$ to every $x$ by continuity and full support of $\pi$.  
The Lebesgue density is $p_t(x,y)=\kappa_t(x,y)w(y)$. For fixed $t>0$, both factors are continuous and strictly positive on the compact set $\mathcal C^2$. Consequently,
$$
0<\min_{x,y\in\mathcal C}p_t(x,y)\leq\max_{x,y\in\mathcal C}p_t(x,y)<\infty,
$$
which proves the asserted extrema.

title: Proof
body_md:
By Proposition~\ref{prop:continuous:structure}~(ii), $P_t$ is self adjoint on $L^2(\pi)$ and satisfies $P_t1=1$. Hence, for every bounded measurable $f$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
    \int_{\mathcal C}P_tf\,d\pi
    &=\langle1,P_tf\rangle_{L^2(\pi)} =\langle P_t1,f\rangle_{L^2(\pi)} =\int_{\mathcal C}f\,d\pi.
\end{aligned}
$$
Thus $\pi$ is invariant.  
To prove uniqueness, fix $t>0$. Proposition~\ref{prop:continuous:structure}~(iii) gives a jointly continuous, strictly positive transition density on $\mathcal C^2$. Since $\pi(dy)=w(y)dy$ with $w$ continuous and strictly positive, the density $\kappa_t(x,y)=dP_t(x,\cdot)/d\pi(y)$ has the same properties. Compactness therefore gives $\min_{x,y\in\mathcal C}\kappa_t(x,y)>0$. Set $\varepsilon_t=\frac12\min_{x,y\in\mathcal C}\kappa_t(x,y)$. Since $\int_{\mathcal C}\kappa_t(x,y)\pi(dy)=1$, we have $0<\varepsilon_t\leq1/2$. Thus
$$
P_t(x,dy)=\varepsilon_t\pi(dy)+(1-\varepsilon_t)\frac{\kappa_t(x,y)-\varepsilon_t}{1-\varepsilon_t}\pi(dy).
$$
The second fraction defines a Markov kernel, which contracts total variation. If $\nu$ is another invariant probability measure, then
$$
\mathrm{TV}(\nu,\pi)=\mathrm{TV}(\nu P_t,\pi P_t)\leq(1-\varepsilon_t)\mathrm{TV}(\nu,\pi).
$$
Since $\varepsilon_t>0$, this forces $\mathrm{TV}(\nu,\pi)=0$, proving uniqueness.

title: Proof
body_md:
First, a finite Poincar\'e constant exists under the stated assumptions. The density $w=Z^{-1}e^{-U}$ has bounds $0<w_{\min}\leq w\leq w_{\max}<\infty$. Let $C_{\mathcal C}$ be a Lebesgue Poincar\'e constant on the bounded convex domain and $f_{\mathcal C}=|\mathcal C|^{-1}\int_{\mathcal C}f\,dx$. For $f\in H^1(\mathcal C)$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}_\pi(f)
&\leq w_{\max}\int_{\mathcal C}|f-f_{\mathcal C}|^2dx\leq w_{\max}C_{\mathcal C}\int_{\mathcal C}\|\nabla f\|^2dx
\leq\frac{w_{\max}}{w_{\min}}C_{\mathcal C}\int_{\mathcal C}\|\nabla f\|^2d\pi.
\end{aligned}
$$
Thus $C_P=(w_{\max}/w_{\min})C_{\mathcal C}$ is admissible. The convergence argument below uses any valid $C_P$, not necessarily this bound. Denote $h_0:=d\mu_0/d\pi$. The assumption $\chi^2(\mu_0\Vert\pi)<\infty$ gives $h_0\in L^2(\pi)$. Since the semigroup is self adjoint by Proposition~\ref{prop:continuous:structure}~(ii), the density evolves according to
$$
    h_t=P_t^*h_0=P_th_0.
$$
For every $t>0$, Proposition~\ref{prop:continuous:structure}~(ii) gives $h_t\in\mathcal D(\mathcal L)$. Since $P_t1=1$ and $\int h_0d\pi=1$, one has $\int h_td\pi=1$. Therefore
$$
\begin{aligned}
    \frac{d}{dt}\chi^2(\mu_t\Vert\pi)
    &=\frac{d}{dt}\|h_t-1\|_{L^2(\pi)}^2
    =2\langle h_t-1,\mathcal Lh_t\rangle_{L^2(\pi)}\\
    &=2\langle h_t,\mathcal Lh_t\rangle_{L^2(\pi)} =-2\mathcal E(h_t,h_t) =-2\int_{\mathcal C}e^{U-U_0}\|\nabla h_t\|^2d\pi.
\end{aligned}
$$
By the definition of $\alpha_0$ and the Poincar\'e inequality,
$$
\begin{aligned}
    \mathcal E(h_t,h_t)
    &\geq\alpha_0\int_{\mathcal C}\|\nabla h_t\|^2d\pi
    \geq\frac{\alpha_0}{C_P}\operatorname{Var}_\pi(h_t)\\
    &=\frac{\alpha_0}{C_P}\|h_t-1\|_{L^2(\pi)}^2 =\frac{\alpha_0}{C_P}\chi^2(\mu_t\Vert\pi).
\end{aligned}
$$
Hence, for every $t>0$,
$$
    \frac{d}{dt}\chi^2(\mu_t\Vert\pi)
    \leq-\frac{2\alpha_0}{C_P}\chi^2(\mu_t\Vert\pi).
$$
Applying Gr\"{o}nwall's inequality on $[s,t]$ with $0<s<t$ gives
$$
    \chi^2(\mu_t\Vert\pi)
    \leq e^{-2\alpha_0(t-s)/C_P}\chi^2(\mu_s\Vert\pi).
$$
Strong continuity of $P_s$ on $L^2(\pi)$ yields $h_s\to h_0$ in $L^2(\pi)$ as $s\to0$. Letting $s\to0$ proves
$$
    \chi^2(\mu_t\Vert\pi)
    \leq e^{-2\alpha_0t/C_P}\chi^2(\mu_0\Vert\pi).
$$
This completes the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
We adapt the proof of Lemma 2.3 in~\cite{bubeck2018sampling}. Let $N:=\lceil T/\eta\rceil$. For $i=0,\dots,N-1$, define
$$
Y_i:=\sup_{u\in[i\eta,(i+2)\eta]}
\left\|W_u-W_{(i+1)\eta}\right\|.
$$

We first reduce the modulus of continuity to $\max_{0\leq i\leq N-1}Y_i$. Fix $s,t\in[0,T]$ with $|t-s|\leq\eta$. By symmetry, assume $s\leq t$. If $s=T$, then $s=t$. Otherwise, let $i=\lfloor s/\eta\rfloor\leq N-1$. Then $s,t\in[i\eta,(i+2)\eta]$ and by the triangle inequality,
$$
\|W_t-W_s\|
\leq \left\|W_t-W_{(i+1)\eta}\right\|+\left\|W_s-W_{(i+1)\eta}\right\|
\leq 2Y_i
\leq 2\max_{0\leq j\leq N-1}Y_j.
$$
Taking the supremum over $|t-s|\leq \eta$ yields
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:reduce_to_Y}
    \sup_{s,t\in[0,T],|t-s|\leq \eta}\|W_t-W_s\|^2 \leq 4\max_{0\leq i\leq N-1}Y_i^2.
\end{equation}
Next, we bound $\mathbb E\left[ \max_{0\leq i\leq N-1}Y_i^2 \right]$ via an $L^p$ maximal inequality. For any $p\geq 1$, by Jensen's inequality,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:max_lp}
    \mathbb E\left[ \max_{0\leq i\leq N-1}Y_i^2 \right]
    \leq \mathbb E\left[ \left( \sum_{i=0}^{N-1}Y_i^{2p} \right)^{1/p} \right]
    \leq \left( \mathbb E\left[ \sum_{i=0}^{N-1}Y_i^{2p} \right] \right)^{1/p}
    \leq N^{1/p}\|Y_0^2\|_p
    =N^{1/p}\|Y_0\|_{2p}^2,
\end{equation}
where we used the fact that $(Y_i)_{i\geq 0}$ are identically distributed by stationary increments. We now bound $\|Y_0\|_{2p}$. Note that
$$
Y_0=\sup_{u\in[0,2\eta]}\|W_u-W_{\eta}\|
\leq \sup_{v\in[0,\eta]}\|W_{\eta+v}-W_{\eta}\|
   +\sup_{v\in[0,\eta]}\|W_{\eta}-W_{\eta-v}\|.
$$
By stationary increments and time reversal, both suprema on the right hand side have the same distribution as $\sup_{v\in[0,\eta]}\|W_v\|$. Hence, by Minkowski's inequality,
$$
\|Y_0\|_{2p}\leq 2\left\Vert \sup_{v\in[0,\eta]}\|W_v\| \right\Vert _{2p}.
$$
Since $\|\cdot\|$ is convex and $W_u$ is a martingale, the process $M_u:=\|W_u\|$ is a nonnegative submartingale. Thus, by Doob's maximal inequality, for $p\geq 1$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:doob}
\|Y_0\|_{2p}
\leq 2\left\Vert \sup_{u\in[0,\eta]} M_u \right\Vert _{2p}
\leq 4\|M_\eta\|_{2p}
=4\|\,\|W_\eta\|\,\|_{2p}.
\end{equation}
Since $W_\eta\stackrel{d}{=}\sqrt{\eta}\,G$ with $G\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_d)$, standard Gaussian moment bounds imply that for $p\geq 2$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:gauss_moment}
\|\,\|W_\eta\|\,\|_{2p}^2
=\eta\,\|\,\|G\|\,\|_{2p}^2
\leq c_1\,\eta\, d\, p,
\end{equation}
for a universal constant $c_1>0$. Combining \eqref{eq:doob} and \eqref{eq:gauss_moment}, we obtain for $p\geq 2$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Y0_bound}
\|Y_0\|_{2p}^2 \leq c_2\,\eta\, d\, p,
\end{equation}
with a universal constant $c_2>0$. Plugging \eqref{eq:Y0_bound} into \eqref{eq:max_lp} gives
$$
\mathbb{E}\left[\max_{0\leq i\leq N-1} Y_i^2\right]
\leq c_2\, N^{1/p}\,\eta\, d\, p.
$$
Choose $p:=\lceil \log N\rceil$. Since $T/\eta\geq e$, we have $N\geq3$ and hence $p\geq2$. Also $N^{1/p}\leq e$. Moreover, $N\leq T/\eta+1\leq2T/\eta$ and $\log(T/\eta)\geq1$, so
\begin{equation}
p\leq\log N+1
\leq\log(T/\eta)+\log2+1
\leq(2+\log2)\log(T/\eta).
\end{equation}
Thus,
$$
\mathbb{E}\left[\max_{0\leq i\leq N-1} Y_i^2\right]
\leq c_3\, \eta\, d\, \log(T/\eta),
$$
for a universal constant $c_3>0$. Finally, using \eqref{eq:reduce_to_Y},
$$
\mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{s,t\in[0,T],|t-s|\leq \eta}\|W_t-W_s\|^2\right]
\leq 4\,\mathbb{E}\left[\max_{0\leq i\leq N-1} Y_i^2\right]
\leq C\, d\,\eta\log(T/\eta),
$$
where $C:=4c_3$ is a universal constant. This completes the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
We first estimate the continuous regulator $\hat K$. Since $\operatorname{dist}(X_0,\partial\mathcal C)\geq r_0$ almost surely, $B(X_0,r_0)\subset\mathcal C$ almost surely. For $\hat L(ds)$ almost every $s$, the point $X_0+r_0\hat\nu_s$ belongs to $\mathcal C$. Since $\hat\nu_s\in N_{\mathcal C}^{\rm out}(\hat X_s)$, we have $\left\langle\hat\nu_s,X_0+r_0\hat\nu_s-\hat X_s\right\rangle\leq0$. Hence,
$$
\left\langle\hat X_s-X_0,\hat\nu_s\right\rangle
\geq r_0.
$$
And thus, we can get
\begin{align}
\int_0^t\left\langle\hat X_s-X_0,d\hat K_s\right\rangle
\geq r_0|\hat K|_t.\label{eq:hat:K:normal:lower}
\end{align}
Define
\begin{align}
\widehat D_t
&:=\int_0^t\left\langle\hat X_s-X_0, \, b\left(\bar X_{\lfloor s/\eta\rfloor\eta}\right)\right\rangle ds, \qquad
\widehat M_t:=\int_0^t\left\langle\hat X_s-X_0,
\sqrt2\sigma\left(\bar X_{\lfloor s/\eta\rfloor\eta}\right)dW_s\right\rangle,\nonumber\\
\widehat Q_t
&:=\int_0^t
\left\|\sqrt2\sigma\left(\bar X_{\lfloor s/\eta\rfloor\eta}\right)I_d\right\|_{\rm F}^2ds.
\end{align}
Since $\hat K$ has finite variation, the trace of the quadratic variation of $\hat X$ is $\widehat Q_t$. It\^o's formula, integrated from $0$ to $t$ with $\hat X_0=X_0$, therefore gives
\begin{equation}
\left\|\hat X_t-X_0\right\|^2
=2\widehat D_t+2\widehat M_t
-2\int_0^t\left\langle\hat X_s-X_0,d\hat K_s\right\rangle
+\widehat Q_t.\label{eq:hat:K:Ito:integrated}
\end{equation}
By \eqref{eq:hat:K:normal:lower} and \eqref{eq:hat:K:Ito:integrated},
\begin{align}
2r_0|\hat K|_t
&\leq2\widehat D_t+2\widehat M_t+\widehat Q_t
-\left\|\hat X_t-X_0\right\|^2
\leq2|\widehat D_t|+2|\widehat M_t|+\widehat Q_t.\label{eq:hat:K:pathwise}
\end{align}
Because $\hat X_s,X_0\in\mathcal C\subset B(0,R)$, the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, It\^o's isometry, and \eqref{eqn:b:sigma:bdd} yield
\begin{align}
|\widehat D_t|^2
&\leq\left(\int_0^t2RB_bds\right)^2
=4R^2B_b^2t^2,\label{eq:hat:K:D}\\
\mathbb E|\widehat M_t|^2
&=2\mathbb E\int_0^t
\left\|\sigma\left(\bar X_{\lfloor s/\eta\rfloor\eta}\right)
\left(\hat X_s-X_0\right)\right\|^2ds\nonumber\\
&\leq2\mathbb E\int_0^t
\left\|\sigma\left(\bar X_{\lfloor s/\eta\rfloor\eta}\right)I_d\right\|_{\rm op}^2
\left\|\hat X_s-X_0\right\|^2ds
\leq8R^2S_\sigma^2t,\label{eq:hat:K:M}\\
\widehat Q_t^2
&\leq\left(\int_0^t2S_\sigma^2ds\right)^2
=4S_\sigma^4t^2.\label{eq:hat:K:Q}
\end{align}
Using $(a+b+c)^2\leq3(a^2+b^2+c^2)$ in \eqref{eq:hat:K:pathwise}, we conclude that
\begin{align}
\mathbb E|\hat K|_t^2
&\leq3r_0^{-2}\left(
\mathbb E|\widehat D_t|^2+\mathbb E|\widehat M_t|^2
+\frac14\mathbb E\widehat Q_t^2\right)\nonumber\\
&\leq3r_0^{-2}\left(4R^2B_b^2+S_\sigma^4\right)t^2
+24r_0^{-2}R^2S_\sigma^2t
:=At^2+Bt.\label{eq:hat:K:proof:final}
\end{align}
Now we compute the bound on the discretization grid. Let $t_j=j\eta$ and write
\begin{equation}\label{eq:discrete:increment:proof}
u_j:=\eta b\left(\bar X_{t_{j-1}}\right)
+\sqrt2\sigma\left(\bar X_{t_{j-1}}\right)\Delta W_j,
\qquad
k_j:=\Delta\bar K_j,
\qquad
\Delta W_j:=W_{t_j}-W_{t_{j-1}}.
\end{equation}
By~\eqref{eq:discrete:regulator:increment},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:discrete:update:proof}
\bar X_{t_j}=\bar X_{t_{j-1}}+u_j-k_j,
\qquad
k_j\in N_{\mathcal C}^{\rm out}(\bar X_{t_j}).
\end{equation}
On $\{k_j\neq0\}$, the point $X_0+r_0k_j/\|k_j\|$ belongs to $\mathcal C$. Hence, the definition of the outward normal cone implies
\begin{align}
\left\langle k_j,
X_0+r_0\frac{k_j}{\|k_j\|}-\bar X_{t_j}\right\rangle \leq 0,
\qquad
\left\langle\bar X_{t_j}-X_0,k_j\right\rangle
\geq r_0\|k_j\|.\label{eq:projection:interior:ball}
\end{align}
The same inequality is immediate when $k_j=0$. Expanding the square in \eqref{eq:discrete:update:proof} gives
\begin{align}
\left\|\bar X_{t_j}-X_0\right\|^2
=\left\|\bar X_{t_{j-1}}-X_0\right\|^2
+2\left\langle\bar X_{t_{j-1}}-X_0,u_j\right\rangle+\|u_j\|^2
-2\left\langle\bar X_{t_j}-X_0,k_j\right\rangle-\|k_j\|^2.\label{eq:discrete:energy:identity}
\end{align}
Summing~\eqref{eq:discrete:energy:identity} from $j=1$ to $k$, using $\bar X_0=X_0$, and applying~\eqref{eq:projection:interior:ball}, we obtain
\begin{align}
2r_0\sum_{j=1}^k\|k_j\|
\leq2\sum_{j=1}^k
\left\langle\bar X_{t_{j-1}}-X_0,u_j\right\rangle
+\sum_{j=1}^k\|u_j\|^2
\leq2|D_T|+2|M_T|+Q_T,\label{eq:bar:K:pathwise}
\end{align}
where
\begin{align}
&D_T:=\sum_{j=1}^k\eta
\left\langle\bar X_{t_{j-1}}-X_0,b\left(\bar X_{t_{j-1}}\right)\right\rangle,\\
&M_T:=\sum_{j=1}^k
\left\langle\bar X_{t_{j-1}}-X_0,
\sqrt2\sigma\left(\bar X_{t_{j-1}}\right)\Delta W_j\right\rangle,\quad
Q_T:=\sum_{j=1}^k\|u_j\|^2.
\end{align}
Since $|\bar K|_T=\sum_{j=1}^k\|k_j\|$, the drift bound and the discrete It\^o isometry give
\begin{align}
|D_T|^2
&\leq\left(\sum_{j=1}^k2RB_b\eta\right)^2
=4R^2B_b^2T^2,\label{eq:bar:K:D}\\
\mathbb E|M_T|^2
&=2\sum_{j=1}^k\eta\,
\mathbb E\left[
\sigma\left(\bar X_{t_{j-1}}\right)^2
\left\|\bar X_{t_{j-1}}-X_0\right\|^2\right]
\leq8R^2S_\sigma^2T.\label{eq:bar:K:M}
\end{align}
For the last term, \eqref{eqn:b:sigma:bdd} implies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:bar:K:Q:pathwise}
Q_T
\leq2B_b^2T\eta
+\frac{4S_\sigma^2}{d}Q_W,
\qquad
Q_W:=\sum_{j=1}^k\|\Delta W_j\|^2.
\end{equation}
Since $Q_W/\eta$ has the chi squared distribution with $kd$ degrees of freedom,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:QW:second:moment}
\mathbb E\left[Q_W^2\right]
=\eta^2\bigl((kd)^2+2kd\bigr)
=d^2T^2+2dT\eta.
\end{equation}
Using $(a+b)^2\leq2a^2+2b^2$, $d\geq1$, and $0<\eta\leq1$ in \eqref{eq:bar:K:Q:pathwise} yields
\begin{align}
\mathbb E\left[Q_T^2\right]
\leq8B_b^4T^2\eta^2
+\frac{32S_\sigma^4}{d^2}\mathbb E Q_W^2
\leq\left(8B_b^4+32S_\sigma^4\right)T^2+64S_\sigma^4T.
\label{eq:bar:K:Q}
\end{align}
Finally,~\eqref{eq:bar:K:pathwise} and $(a+b+c)^2\leq3(a^2+b^2+c^2)$ give
\begin{align}
\mathbb E\left[|\bar K|_T^2\right]
&\leq3r_0^{-2}\left(
\mathbb E|D_T|^2+\mathbb E|M_T|^2+\frac14\mathbb E Q_T^2
\right)\nonumber\\
&\leq3r_0^{-2}\left(4R^2B_b^2+2B_b^4+8S_\sigma^4\right)T^2
+3r_0^{-2}\left(8R^2S_\sigma^2+16S_\sigma^4\right)T
=\bar A T^2+\bar B T.
\end{align}
This completes the proof.

&\leq

+\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mathrm{Law}(x_{k}),\mathrm{Law}(X_{k\eta}))

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix an interior ball $B(z,r)\subset\mathcal C$, and write
$$
D:=\operatorname{diam}(\mathcal C), \quad S:=\sup_{x\in\mathcal C}\|\sigma(x)I_d\|_{\mathrm F}.
$$
Use the bridge $\hat X$ from \eqref{eqn:hat:x} with $b=0$. The regulator estimates in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lemma:bound:K} use only bounded coefficients and an interior ball. To allow every initial point, expand the squared distance to $z$, rather than to $X_0$. The initial squared distance is then at most $D^2$. The same continuous and discrete energy identities give
$$
r|\hat K|_s\leq D^2/2+|\hat M_s|+S^2s,\qquad r|\bar K|_s\leq D^2/2+|\bar M_s|+\tfrac12 Q_s,
$$
Here, with $\Delta W_{j+1}:=W_{(j+1)\eta}-W_{j\eta}$, the martingale terms are
$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat M_s:=\int_0^s\left\langle\hat X_u-z,
\sqrt2\sigma\left(\bar X_{\lfloor u/\eta\rfloor\eta}\right)\,dW_u\right\rangle,\quad \bar M_s:=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\left\langle\bar X_{j\eta}-z,
\sqrt2\sigma\left(\bar X_{j\eta}\right)\Delta W_{j+1}\right\rangle,
\end{aligned}
$$
and 
\[
Q_s:=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\left\|\sqrt2\sigma\left(\bar X_{j\eta}\right)\Delta W_{j+1}\right\|^2.
\]
Since the states lie in $\mathcal C$ and the coefficients are bounded, It\^o's isometry and orthogonality of the discrete martingale increments give $\mathbb E|\hat M_s|^2,\mathbb E|\bar M_s|^2\leq2D^2S^2s$. Since $\sigma$ is scalar,
$$
Q_s\leq\frac{2S^2}{d}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\|\Delta W_{j+1}\|^2,\qquad
\mathbb E Q_s^2\leq4S^4(s^2+2s\eta/d)\leq12S^4s^2.
$$
Consequently,
\begin{align}
\mathbb E\left[|\hat K|_s^2\right]&\leq
R_{\rm c}(s):=3r^{-2}\left(D^4/4+2D^2S^2s+S^4s^2\right),\nonumber\\
\mathbb E\left[|\bar K|_s^2\right]&\leq
R_{\rm d}(s):=3r^{-2}\left(D^4/4+2D^2S^2s+3S^4s^2\right).
\label{eq:const:regulator:bounds}
\end{align}
These bounds are uniform over $X_0\in\mathcal C$, in particular, they do not require the initial law to avoid the boundary. The Brownian maximum argument of Lemma~\ref{lemma:bound:bm}, applied on the $n$ grid intervals, yields
$$
\mathbb E\left[\max_{0\leq j<n}\sup_{j\eta\leq t\leq(j+1)\eta}
\|W_t-W_{j\eta}\|^2\right]\leq C_{\rm B}d\eta(1+\log n)
$$
for a universal $C_{\rm B}$. Indeed, the one dimensional reflection bound, followed by a union bound over intervals and integration of the tail, gives $C_{\rm B}\eta(1 + \log n)$ per coordinate. This version holds for every $s>0$. Thus,
$$
\mathbb E\left[\sup_{t\leq s}\left\|\bar Y_t-\hat Y_t\right\|^2\right]\leq\beta\eta(1+\log n),\qquad \beta:=2C_{\rm B}S^2.
$$
The convex Skorokhod comparison \eqref{eq:slominski:bridge:comparison} and Cauchy-Schwarz inequality give
$$
\mathbb E\left[\sup_{t\leq s}\left\|\bar X_t-\hat X_t\right\|^2\right]
\leq\beta\eta(1+\log n)+4\sqrt{\beta\eta(1+\log n)}\,V_s,\qquad
V_s:=\sqrt{R_{\rm c}(s)}+\sqrt{R_{\rm d}(s)}.
$$
Since $(1 + \log n)\leq n$, we have $\eta(1+\log n)\leq n\eta=s$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:const:Is}
G_s:=\beta\sqrt s+4\sqrt\beta\,V_s,\qquad
I_s:=\left(1+\sqrt{e^{4\ell_\sigma^2s}-1}\right)\sqrt{G_s}.
\end{equation}
The bridge error is at most $G_s\sqrt{\eta(1+\log n)}$. For $f(t)=\mathbb E\|X_t-\hat X_t\|^2$, the reflection sign already proved in \eqref{Skorokhod:ineqn}, It\^o's formula, and coefficient Lipschitz continuity imply
$$
f(t)\leq4\ell_\sigma^2\int_0^t\left(f(u)+G_s\sqrt{\eta(1+\log n)}\right)\,du,\qquad t\leq s.
$$
Therefore, Gr\"{o}nwall's inequlity gives
\[
f(s)\leq\left(e^{4\ell_\sigma^2s}-1\right)G_s\sqrt{\eta(1+\log n)}.
\]
This formula also holds when $\ell_\sigma=0$, since then $f(s)=0$. The synchronous construction and the $L^2$ triangle inequality now yield
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal W_2\left(\mathrm{Law}(\bar X_s),\mathrm{Law}(X_s)\right)
&\leq\left(\mathbb E\left\|\bar X_s-\hat X_s\right\|^2\right)^{1/2}+\left(f(s)\right)^{1/2}\\
&\leq\left(1+\sqrt{e^{4\ell_\sigma^2s}-1}\right)\sqrt{G_s}[\eta(1+\log n)]^{1/4}\\
&:=I_s[\eta(1+\log(s/\eta))]^{1/4}.
\end{aligned}
$$
The estimates are uniform over the initial point in $\mathcal C$. Conditioning on any common initial law and integrating preserves the same bound, proving~\eqref{eq:const:strong:euler:log-rate}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Synchronous coupling, the convex reflection sign, and It\^o's formula give $\mathbb E\|X_t^x-X_t^y\|^2\leq e^{2\ell_\sigma^2t}\|x-y\|^2$. Integrating over a coupling of the initial laws proves \eqref{eq:const:short:stability}. For smooth $u$, integration along the segment in $\mathcal C$ and Cauchy-Schwarz inequality give
$$
|P_su(y)-P_su(x)|\leq\bigl(\mathbb E\|X_s^y-X_s^x\|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\left(\mathbb E\int_0^1\left\|\nabla u\left((1-\theta)X_s^x+\theta X_s^y\right)\right\|^2d\theta\right)^{1/2}.
$$
The mean square bound gives $X_s^y\to X_s^x$ in probability as $y\to x$. Dividing by $\|y-x\|$ and using bounded uniform continuity of $\nabla u$ yields
$$
\limsup_{\substack{y\to x\\y\in\mathcal C,\ y\neq x}}
\frac{|P_su(y)-P_su(x)|}{\|y-x\|}
\leq e^{\ell_\sigma^2s}\bigl[P_s(|\nabla u|^2)(x)\bigr]^{1/2}.
$$
The kernel bound $\kappa_s\leq M_s$ and integration of local slopes along segments yield
\begin{equation}\label{eq:const:H1:smoothing}
\operatorname{Lip}(P_su)\leq e^{\ell_\sigma^2s}\sqrt{M_s}\,
\|\nabla u\|_{L^2(\pi)}.
\end{equation}
Smooth approximation in $H^1(\mathcal C)$ and $\|P_sv\|_\infty\leq\sqrt{M_s}\|v\|_2$ extend \eqref{eq:const:H1:smoothing} to $u\in H^1(\mathcal C)$. Spectral calculus for $-\mathcal L$ from Proposition~\ref{prop:continuous:structure}~(ii) gives, for $\pi(f)=0$ and $v\geq0$,
$$
\mathcal E(P_{s+v}f,P_{s+v}f)
\leq\frac{1}{2es}\|P_vf\|_2^2
\leq\frac{e^{-2g_0v}}{2es}\|f\|_2^2,
$$
because $\sup_{z\geq0}ze^{-2sz}=1/(2es)$ and the spectral gap is at least $g_0$. Using $\mathcal E(u,u)\geq\lambda\|\nabla u\|_2^2$ in \eqref{eq:const:H1:smoothing}, we obtain
$$
\operatorname{Lip}(P_tf)
\leq e^{\ell_\sigma^2s}\sqrt{\frac{M_s}{2es\lambda}}\,
e^{-g_0(t-2s)}\|f\|_2,\qquad t\geq2s.
$$
To pass from test functions to densities, first note that the heat kernel bound makes $\mu P_t$ and $\nu P_t$ have bounded densities for $t\geq s$. Their difference has zero integral. For any mean zero $f\in L^2(\pi)$ with $\|f\|_2\leq1$,
$$
\left|\int_{\mathcal C}f\,d(\mu P_t-\nu P_t)\right|=\left|\int_{\mathcal C}P_tf\,d(\mu-\nu)\right|\leq\operatorname{Lip}(P_tf)\mathcal W_1(\mu,\nu).
$$
Taking the supremum over these test functions gives the $L^2(\pi)$ norm of the density difference. Combining the preceding Lipschitz estimate with $\mathcal W_1(\mu,\nu)\leq\mathcal W_2(\mu,\nu)$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:const:density:stability}
\left\|\frac{d(\mu P_t-\nu P_t)}{d\pi}\right\|_2
\leq e^{\ell_\sigma^2s}\sqrt{\frac{M_s}{2es\lambda}}\,
e^{-g_0(t-2s)}\mathcal W_2(\mu,\nu).
\end{equation}
For probability densities $a,b\in L^2(\pi)$ with $a,b\geq m>0$, solve the weak Neumann equation
$$
\int_{\mathcal{C}}\nabla\psi\cdot\nabla v\,d\pi=\int_{\mathcal{C}}(b-a)v\,d\pi,\qquad \pi(\psi)=0.
$$
On the mean zero subspace of $H^1(\mathcal C)$, the Poincar\'e inequality makes the gradient form coercive, so Lax-Milgram~\cite[Corollary~5.8]{brezis2011functional} gives a unique mean zero solution. Taking $v=\psi$ in its weak equation gives
$$
\|\nabla\psi\|_2^2=\int_{\mathcal C}(b-a)\psi\,d\pi\leq\|b-a\|_2\|\psi\|_2\leq\sqrt{C_P}\|b-a\|_2\|\nabla\psi\|_2.
$$
Dividing when $\|\nabla\psi\|_2>0$, with the zero case immediate, yields $\|\nabla\psi\|_2^2\leq C_P\|a-b\|_2^2$. For the density path $a_\theta=(1-\theta)a+\theta b$, the flux $(d\pi/dx)\nabla\psi$ satisfies the weak continuity equation with zero boundary flux. The Benamou-Brenier action bound~\cite{benamou2000computational} gives
$$
\mathcal W_2^2(a\pi,b\pi)
\leq\int_0^1\int_{\mathcal{C}}\frac{|\nabla\psi|^2}{a_\theta}\,d\pi\,d\theta
\leq\frac{C_P}{m}\|a-b\|_2^2.
$$
This weak formulation requires no differentiability of $d\pi/dx$, see \cite[Section~2]{peyre2018comparison}. For $t\geq s$, the semigroup property gives $m_s\leq\kappa_t\leq M_s$, so the densities of $\mu P_t,\nu P_t$ lie in $L^2(\pi)$ and are bounded below by $m_s$ for arbitrary initial laws. Applying the transport estimate to the densities of $\mu P_t$ and $\nu P_t$, then using~\eqref{eq:const:density:stability}, gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal W_2(\mu P_t,\nu P_t)&\leq\sqrt{\frac{C_P}{m_s}}\left\|\frac{d(\mu P_t-\nu P_t)}{d\pi}\right\|_2\\
&\leq e^{\ell_\sigma^2s}\sqrt{\frac{C_PM_s}{2es\lambda m_s}}e^{-g_0(t-2s)}\mathcal W_2(\mu,\nu)\\
&=H_se^{-g_0(t-2s)}\mathcal W_2(\mu,\nu),
\end{aligned}
$$
since $g_0=\lambda/C_P$ and $H_s$ is defined in~\eqref{eq:const:heatkernel:constants}. This proves~\eqref{eq:const:long:stability}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $Q_\eta$ denote one projected Euler-Maruyama step and $Q=Q_\eta^n$. Proposition~\ref{prop:const:strong:euler}, conditioned on the initial state, gives for every probability measure $\nu$ on $\mathcal C$
$$
\mathcal W_2(\nu Q,\nu P_s)\leq
\delta_s:=I_s[\eta(1+\log(s/\eta))]^{1/4}.
$$
Set $\rho_i:=\mu_0Q^iP_{(m-i)s}$ for $i=0,\ldots,m$, so that $\rho_0=\mu_0P_{ms}$ and $\rho_m=\mu_0Q^m$. For $i=1,\ldots,m$, write $\nu_i:=\mu_0Q^{i-1}$ and $j=m-i$. The semigroup property gives
$$
\rho_i=(\nu_iQ)P_{js},\qquad
\rho_{i-1}=(\nu_iP_s)P_{js}.
$$
Since $\mathcal W_2(\nu_iQ,\nu_iP_s)\leq\delta_s$, Lemma~\ref{lem:const:semigroup:stability} yields
$$
\mathcal W_2(\rho_i,\rho_{i-1})
\leq\delta_s
\begin{cases}
1,&j=0,\\
e^{\ell_\sigma^2s},&j=1,\\
H_se^{-g_0(j-2)s},&j\geq2.
\end{cases}
$$
For $m\geq3$, the triangle inequality and the change of index $j=m-i$ give
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal W_2\left(\mu_0Q^m,\mu_0P_{ms}\right)&\leq\sum_{i=1}^m\mathcal W_2(\rho_i,\rho_{i-1})\\
&\leq\delta_s\left(1+e^{\ell_\sigma^2s}+H_s\sum_{j=2}^{m-1}e^{-g_0(j-2)s}\right)\\
&\leq\delta_s\left(1+e^{\ell_\sigma^2s}+H_s\sum_{j=2}^{\infty}e^{-g_0(j-2)s}\right)\\
&=\delta_s\left(1+e^{\ell_\sigma^2s}+\frac{H_s}{1-e^{-g_0s}}\right)=B_s\delta_s.
\end{aligned}
$$
For $m=1$, only $j=0$ occurs, while for $m=2$ only $j=0,1$ occur. The same triangle inequality therefore gives
$$
\mathcal W_2\left(\mu_0Q,\mu_0P_s\right)\leq\delta_s\leq B_s\delta_s,\quad
\mathcal W_2\left(\mu_0Q^2,\mu_0P_{2s}\right)\leq\delta_s\left(1+e^{\ell_\sigma^2s}\right)\leq B_s\delta_s.
$$
Thus the estimate holds for every integer $m\geq1$. To identify the numerical law, use the one step transition kernel $Q_\eta$ and the initial law $\mathrm{Law}(\bar X_0)=\mu_0$. For every Borel set $A\subseteq\mathcal C$ and integer $k\geq0$, the Markov property gives
$$
\mathbb P(\bar X_{(k+1)\eta}\in A)=\int_{\mathcal C}Q_\eta(x,A)\,\mathrm{Law}(\bar X_{k\eta})(dx).
$$
Induction yields $\mathrm{Law}(\bar X_{k\eta})=\mu_0Q_\eta^k$. Since $Q=Q_\eta^n$ and $n\eta=s$,
$$
\mu_0Q^m=\mu_0(Q_\eta^n)^m=\mu_0Q_\eta^{nm}=\mathrm{Law}(\bar X_{nm\eta})=\mathrm{Law}(\bar X_{ms}).
$$
Substituting this identity, $T=ms$, the definition of $\delta_s$, and $F_s=B_sI_s$ into the preceding estimate gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal W_2\left(\mathrm{Law}(\bar X_T),\mu_0P_T\right)&=\mathcal W_2\left(\mu_0Q^m,\mu_0P_{ms}\right)\\
&\leq B_s\delta_s=B_sI_s\left[\eta\left(1+\log\frac{s}{\eta}\right)\right]^{1/4}
=F_s\left[\eta\left(1+\log\frac{s}{\eta}\right)\right]^{1/4},
\end{aligned}
$$
which proves~\eqref{eq:const:uniform:comparison}.
Under the additional initial $\chi^2$ condition, Corollary~\ref{cor:W:2}, $\alpha_0\geq\lambda$, and $g_0=\lambda/C_P$ give
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal W_2(\mathrm{Law}(\bar X_{ms}),\pi)
&\leq\mathcal W_2(\mu_0Q^m,\mu_0P_{ms}) +\mathcal W_2(\mu_0P_{ms},\pi)\leq B_s\delta_s+A_0e^{-g_0ms/2}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Substituting $F_s=B_sI_s$ and $T=ms$ proves \eqref{eq:const-ref-unconditional-W2}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $\tau=1/g_0$ and $u_x=\kappa_\tau(x,\cdot)-1$. Symmetry and the semigroup identity give, for $v\geq0$,
$$
\pi(u_x)=0,\qquad
\|u_x\|_2^2=\kappa_{2\tau}(x,x)-1,\qquad
\kappa_{2\tau+v}(x,y)-1=\langle u_x,P_vu_y\rangle_2.
$$
In particular, the kernel identities follow by expanding $u_x=\kappa_\tau(x,\cdot)-1$ and applying symmetry and the semigroup property:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\|u_x\|_2^2&=\int_{\mathcal C}\kappa_\tau(x,z)\kappa_\tau(z,x)\pi(dz)-1=\kappa_{2\tau}(x,x)-1,\\
\langle u_x,P_vu_y\rangle_2&=\int_{\mathcal C}\int_{\mathcal C}\kappa_\tau(x,z)\kappa_v(z,w)\kappa_\tau(w,y)\pi(dw)\pi(dz)-1=\kappa_{2\tau+v}(x,y)-1, \quad v>0.
\end{aligned}
$$
For $v=0$, the second identity follows directly from $P_0=I$. Since $\pi(u_y)=0$, the spectral gap gives $\|P_vu_y\|_2\leq e^{-g_0v}\|u_y\|_2$. Consequently,
$$
\left|\langle u_x,P_vu_y\rangle_2\right|\leq e^{-g_0v}\sqrt{\kappa_{2\tau}(x,x)-1}\sqrt{\kappa_{2\tau}(y,y)-1}\leq e^{-g_0v}A_{\rm hk}.
$$
Taking the supremum gives
$$
\sup_{x,y}|\kappa_{2\tau+v}(x,y)-1|
\leq \exp(-g_0v)A_{\rm hk}.
$$
At $v=s_*-2/g_0=g_0^{-1}\log\max\{1,2A_{\rm hk}\}$, the right side is at most $1/2$. Thus $m_{s_*}\geq1/2$ and $M_{s_*}\leq3/2$. Using $s_*=a_*/g_0$ in \eqref{eq:const:heatkernel:constants}, we obtain
$$
\begin{aligned}
H_{s_*} &=\exp(\ell_\sigma^2s_*)\sqrt{\frac{M_{s_*}}{2e\,g_0s_*m_{s_*}}}
\leq\exp\!\left(\frac{\ell_\sigma^2}{g_0}a_*\right)\sqrt{\frac{3/2}{2e\,a_*(1/2)}}\\
&=\exp\!\left(\frac{\ell_\sigma^2}{g_0}a_*\right)\sqrt{\frac{3}{2e\,a_*}}
\leq\exp\!\left(\frac{\ell_\sigma^2}{g_0}a_*\right)\sqrt{\frac{3}{2a_*}}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Since $g_0s_*=a_*\geq2$ and $e^{\ell_\sigma^2s_*}\geq1$, the definitions in~\eqref{eq:const:Fs} and~\eqref{eq:const:Is} give
$$
\begin{aligned}
B_{s_*}&\leq e^{\ell_\sigma^2s_*}\left(2+\frac{\sqrt{3/(2ea_*)}}{1-e^{-a_*}}\right)\leq e^{\ell_\sigma^2s_*}\left(2+\frac{\sqrt{3/(4e)}}{1-e^{-2}}\right)\leq3e^{\ell_\sigma^2s_*},\\
I_{s_*}&=\left(1+\sqrt{e^{4\ell_\sigma^2s_*}-1}\right)\sqrt{G_{s_*}}\leq2e^{2\ell_\sigma^2s_*}\sqrt{G_{s_*}}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Under $\ell_\sigma^2/g_0\leq\ell_*$, their product satisfies
$$
F_{s_*}\leq6\exp\left(3\ell_\sigma^2s_*\right)\sqrt{G_{s_*}}
\leq6\exp(6\ell_*)\max\{1,2A_{\rm hk}\}^{3\ell_*}\sqrt{G_{s_*}},
$$
which proves \eqref{eq:const:conditioning:Fs}. Finally, $\operatorname{Lip}(\sigma)\leq\sqrt\Lambda\,\operatorname{Lip}(U)/2$ gives $\ell_\sigma^2\leq d\Lambda\,\operatorname{Lip}(U)^2/4$, proving the stated sufficient condition.

title: Proof
body_md:
For every $\mu>0$, $g_\mu$ is smooth, $g$ has at most linear growth, while every derivative of the Gaussian kernel is integrable against that growth, locally uniformly in $x$. Differentiation under the convolution integral is therefore valid. Since $g_\mu(x)=\mathbb E[g(x+\mu\xi)]$ and $\xi\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d)$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
    |h_\mu(x)|
    &=\left|g(x)-\mathbb E[g(x+\mu\xi)]\right|\\
    &\leq\mathbb E|g(x)-g(x+\mu\xi)|
    \leq K\mu\mathbb E\|\xi\|
    \leq K\mu\left(\mathbb E\|\xi\|^2\right)^{1/2}
    =K\mu\sqrt d.
\end{aligned}
$$
This proves \eqref{eq:Gaussian:hmu:sup}. For any $x,y\in\mathcal C$, the Lipschitz continuity of $g$ with constant $K$ gives the same Lipschitz bound for $g_\mu$,
\begin{align}
|g_{\mu}(x)-g_{\mu}(y)|
&=\left|\mathbb E\!\left[g(x+\mu\xi)-g(y+\mu\xi)\right]\right|\leq \mathbb E\!\left[
|g(x+\mu\xi)-g(y+\mu\xi)|
\right]\leq K\|x-y\|.
\end{align}
Hence,
\begin{align}
|h_{\mu}(x)-h_{\mu}(y)|
\leq |g(x)-g(y)|+|g_{\mu}(x)-g_{\mu}(y)|\leq 2K\|x-y\|,
\end{align}
which proves~\eqref{eq:Gaussian:hmu:Lipschitz}. Since $g_{\mu}$ is differentiable and Lipschitz with constant $K$, for every unit vector $v\in\mathbb R^d$,
\begin{equation}
|\langle\nabla g_{\mu}(x),v\rangle|
=\lim_{t\to0}
\frac{|g_{\mu}(x+tv)-g_{\mu}(x)|}{|t|}
\leq K.
\end{equation}
Taking the supremum over $\|v\|=1$ gives $\|\nabla g_{\mu}(x)\|\leq K$. Since $0\in\mathcal C\subset B(0,R)$,
\begin{align}
\|\nabla U_{\mu}(x)\|
&\leq \|\nabla f(x)\|+\|\nabla g_{\mu}(x)\|\nonumber\\
&\leq \|\nabla f(0)\|+L_f\|x\|+K
\leq \|\nabla f(0)\|+L_fR+K.
\end{align}
Taking the supremum over $x\in\mathcal C$ proves \eqref{eq:Gaussian:Gmu:explicit}.

It remains to verify the weak convexity and smoothness of $g_\mu$. Fix $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$. Applying the weak convexity inequality with parameter $\rho$ in \eqref{assumption:g:convex:Gaussian:smoothing} to the two points $x+\mu\xi$ and $y+\mu\xi$, we obtain, for every $\xi\in\mathbb R^d$,
\begin{align}
g\!\left(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y+\mu\xi\right)
&=g\!\left(\lambda(x+\mu\xi)
+(1-\lambda)(y+\mu\xi)\right)\nonumber\\
&\leq \lambda g(x+\mu\xi)+(1-\lambda)g(y+\mu\xi)
+\frac{\rho}{2}\lambda(1-\lambda)
\|(x+\mu\xi)-(y+\mu\xi)\|^2\nonumber\\
&=\lambda g(x+\mu\xi)+(1-\lambda)g(y+\mu\xi)
+\frac{\rho}{2}\lambda(1-\lambda)\|x-y\|^2.
\end{align}
Taking expectations with respect to $\xi$ on both sides yields
\begin{align}
g_{\mu}\!\left(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y\right)
&\leq \lambda g_{\mu}(x)+(1-\lambda)g_{\mu}(y)
+\frac{\rho}{2}\lambda(1-\lambda)\|x-y\|^2.
\end{align}
This is precisely the weak convexity inequality with parameter $\rho$ in \eqref{assumption:g:convex:Gaussian:smoothing}. Hence $g_{\mu}$ is weakly convex with parameter $\rho$. Differentiating the Gaussian convolution kernel and using $\mathbb E\xi=0$ gives
$$
    \nabla g_\mu(x)
    =\frac1\mu\mathbb E\left[\xi g(x+\mu\xi)\right] =\frac1\mu\mathbb E\left[\xi\left(g(x+\mu\xi)-g(x)\right)\right].
$$
Consequently,
\begin{align}
\|\nabla g_{\mu}(x)-\nabla g_{\mu}(y)\|
&\leq \frac1\mu\mathbb E\!\left[
\|\xi\|\,|g(x+\mu\xi)-g(y+\mu\xi)|
\right]\leq \frac{K}{\mu}\mathbb E\|\xi\|\,\|x-y\|
\leq \frac{K\sqrt d}{\mu}\|x-y\|.
\end{align}
Since $g_\mu$ is differentiable and weakly convex with parameter $\rho$, the function
$$
    x\mapsto g_\mu(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}\|x\|^2
$$
is differentiable and convex. The monotonicity of its gradient gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
0 &\leq
\left\langle
\nabla g_\mu(x)+\rho x-\nabla g_\mu(y)-\rho y,
x-y
\right\rangle=
\langle\nabla g_\mu(x)-\nabla g_\mu(y),x-y\rangle
+\rho\|x-y\|^2.
\end{aligned}
$$
Therefore,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\langle\nabla U_\mu(x)-\nabla U_\mu(y),x-y\rangle
&=
\langle\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y),x-y\rangle
+\langle\nabla g_\mu(x)-\nabla g_\mu(y),x-y\rangle\\
&\geq(m_f-\rho)\|x-y\|^2.
\end{aligned}
$$
The two gradient Lipschitz bounds also give
$$
\begin{aligned}
\|\nabla U_\mu(x)-\nabla U_\mu(y)\|
&\leq
\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|
+\|\nabla g_\mu(x)-\nabla g_\mu(y)\|\leq
\left(L_f+\frac{K\sqrt d}{\mu}\right)\|x-y\|.
\end{aligned}
$$
The proof is complete.

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $x,y\in\mathcal C$ with $x\neq y$ and define
$$
    r_\mu(x) :=\nabla U_\mu(x)(e^{h_\mu(x)}-1).
$$
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Gaussian:b:perturbation}
    b(x)=-\nabla U_\mu(x)-r_\mu(x).
\end{equation}
By the definition of $\varepsilon_{b,\mu}$,
$$
    \|r_\mu(x)-r_\mu(y)\|
    \leq
    \varepsilon_{b,\mu}\|x-y\|.
$$
Since $U_\mu$ is strongly convex with constant $m_f-\rho$,
\begin{align}
    \langle b(x)-b(y),x-y\rangle
    &=
    -\langle\nabla U_\mu(x)-\nabla U_\mu(y),x-y\rangle
    -\langle r_\mu(x)-r_\mu(y),x-y\rangle
    \nonumber\\
    &\leq
    -(m_f-\rho)\|x-y\|^2
    +\varepsilon_{b,\mu}\|x-y\|^2
    =
    -m_\mu\|x-y\|^2.
    \label{eq:Gaussian:b:dissipativity}
\end{align}
By Lemma~\ref{lemma:propositions of Gaussian smoothing},
$$
    \left\|\nabla U_\mu(x)-\nabla U_\mu(y)\right\|
    \leq
    \left(L_f+\frac{K\sqrt d}{\mu}\right)\|x-y\|.
$$
Combining this estimate with \eqref{eq:Gaussian:b:perturbation} gives
\begin{align}
    \|b(x)-b(y)\|
    &\leq
    \|\nabla U_\mu(x)-\nabla U_\mu(y)\|
    +\|r_\mu(x)-r_\mu(y)\|
    \nonumber\\
    &\leq
    \left(
    L_f+\frac{K\sqrt d}{\mu}
    +\varepsilon_{b,\mu}
    \right)\|x-y\|
   =M_\mu\|x-y\|.
    \label{eq:Gaussian:b:Lipschitz}
\end{align}
Moreover,
\begin{align}
    \left\|\sigma(x)I_d-\sigma(y)I_d\right\|_{\mathrm F}
    =
    \sqrt d\,
    \left|e^{h_\mu(x)/2}-e^{h_\mu(y)/2}\right|
    \leq
    \sqrt d\,\varepsilon_{\sigma,\mu}\|x-y\|
    =
    \sqrt{\alpha_\mu}\|x-y\|.
    \label{eq:Gaussian:sigma:Lipschitz}
\end{align}
It remains to verify the required relations among the constants. From \eqref{eq:Gaussian:perturbation:small},
$$
    \varepsilon_{b,\mu}
    +2\alpha_\mu < m_f-\rho-\frac12.
$$
Therefore
$$
\begin{aligned}
    m_\mu &=m_f-\rho-\varepsilon_{b,\mu}>\frac12+2\alpha_\mu >\alpha_\mu,
\end{aligned}
$$
so $m_\mu>0$ and $0\leq\alpha_\mu<m_\mu$. Hence \eqref{eq:Gaussian:b:dissipativity}, \eqref{eq:Gaussian:b:Lipschitz}, and \eqref{eq:Gaussian:sigma:Lipschitz} verify Assumptions~\ref{asmpt:strongly:convex} and \ref{asmpt:smooth}. Finally,
$$
    2m_\mu-1-4\alpha_\mu = 2\left( m_f-\rho-\frac12 -\varepsilon_{b,\mu} -2\alpha_\mu
    \right)
    = 2\left( m_f-\rho-\frac12 -\varepsilon_{b,\mu} -2d\varepsilon_{\sigma,\mu}^2
    \right)
    >0.
$$
Thus, $2m_\mu>1+4\alpha_\mu$, and all coefficient assumptions of Theorem~\ref{global:error:2} hold.

title: Proof
body_md:
Throughout this proof, $\mathbb E$ denotes expectation with respect to all random variables in the synchronous coupling. For fixed $x\in\mathcal C$, let $\mathbb E_{p_N,k}$ denote expectation only over the $N$ samples $\{\xi_{i,k}\}_{i=1}^N$ used to approximate the Gaussian smoothing function at iteration $k$, and let $\mathbb E_{g_N,k}$ denote expectation only over the $N$ samples $\{\hat\xi_{i,k}\}_{i=1}^N$ used to approximate its gradient. All other quantities are regarded as constants under these two expectations.

Before projection, the difference between the two synchronously coupled algorithms is
\begin{align}
&\tilde x_k-x_k
+\eta\bigl(\tilde b_k(\tilde x_k)-b(x_k)\bigr)
+\sqrt{2\eta}\bigl(\tilde\sigma_k(\tilde x_k)-\sigma(x_k)\bigr)
\xi_{k+1}.
\end{align}
By the nonexpansiveness of the orthogonal projection onto the convex set $\mathcal C$, we obtain
\begin{align}
\mathbb E\|\tilde x_{k+1}-x_{k+1}\|^2
&\leq\mathbb E\Bigl\|\tilde x_k-x_k
+\eta\bigl(\tilde b_k(\tilde x_k)-b(x_k)\bigr)
+\sqrt{2\eta}\bigl(\tilde\sigma_k(\tilde x_k)-\sigma(x_k)\bigr)
\xi_{k+1}\Bigr\|^2
\nonumber\\
&=\mathbb E\Bigl\|\tilde x_k-x_k
+\eta\bigl(b(\tilde x_k)-b(x_k)\bigr)
+\eta\bigl(\tilde b_k(\tilde x_k)-b(\tilde x_k)\bigr)\Bigr\|^2
\nonumber\\
&\quad+2\eta d\,\mathbb E\left[\Bigl|
\sigma(\tilde x_k)-\sigma(x_k)
+\tilde\sigma_k(\tilde x_k)-\sigma(\tilde x_k)\Bigr|^2\right]\nonumber\\
&\leq(1+\eta)\mathbb E
\left[\|\tilde x_k-x_k+\eta(b(\tilde x_k)-b(x_k))\|^2\right]
+\eta(1+\eta)
\mathbb E\left[\left\|\tilde b_k(\tilde x_k)-b(\tilde x_k)\right\|^2\right]\nonumber\\
&\qquad\qquad+4\eta d\,\mathbb E\left[\left|\sigma(\tilde x_k)-\sigma(x_k)\right|^2\right]
+4\eta d\,\mathbb E\left[|\tilde\sigma_k(\tilde x_k)
-\sigma(\tilde x_k)|^2\right],
\label{eq:Gaussian:coupling:first}
\end{align}
where the equality uses that $\xi_{k+1}$ is independent of all quantities at iteration $k$, $\mathbb E[\xi_{k+1}]=0$, and $\mathbb E\|\xi_{k+1}\|^2=d$. The last inequality is obtained by applying $2\langle a,b\rangle\leq\eta\|a\|^2+\eta^{-1}\|b\|^2$ to the first term and applying $|a+b|^2\leq2|a|^2+2|b|^2$ to the second term.

The first term in \eqref{eq:Gaussian:coupling:first} is controlled by the dissipativity and Lipschitz bounds for the ideal drift $b$ in \eqref{eq:Gaussian:b:dissipativity} and \eqref{eq:Gaussian:b:Lipschitz}:
\begin{align}
\|\tilde x_k-x_k+\eta(b(\tilde x_k)-b(x_k))\|^2&=\|\tilde x_k-x_k\|^2
+2\eta\langle\tilde x_k-x_k,b(\tilde x_k)-b(x_k)\rangle
+\eta^2\|b(\tilde x_k)-b(x_k)\|^2\nonumber\\
&\leq(1-2m_\mu\eta+M_\mu^2\eta^2)
\|\tilde x_k-x_k\|^2.
\label{eq:Gaussian:ideal:Euler:contraction}
\end{align}
The third term is controlled directly by the coefficient condition for $\sigma$:
\begin{equation}
d|\sigma(\tilde x_k)-\sigma(x_k)|^2
=\|\sigma(\tilde x_k)I_d-\sigma(x_k)I_d\|_{\mathrm F}^2
\leq\alpha_\mu\|\tilde x_k-x_k\|^2.
\label{eq:Gaussian:ideal:sigma:difference}
\end{equation}
The remaining terms are required to bound the approximation errors from the Monte Carlo simulation. For any fixed $x\in\mathcal C$, decompose the drift and diffusion errors as
\begin{align}
\tilde b_k(x)-b(x)
&=-\bigl(\widetilde{\nabla} U_{\mu,k}(x)-\nabla U_\mu(x)\bigr)
e^{h_\mu(x)-\left(\tilde U_{\mu,k}(x)-U_\mu(x)\right)}\nonumber\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad-\nabla U_\mu(x)e^{h_\mu(x)}
\left(e^{-\left(\tilde U_{\mu,k}(x)-U_\mu(x)\right)}-1\right),
\label{eq:Gaussian:b:MC:difference}\\
\tilde\sigma_k(x)-\sigma(x)
&=e^{h_\mu(x)/2}
\left(e^{-(\tilde U_{\mu,k}(x)-U_\mu(x))/2}-1\right).
\label{eq:Gaussian:sigma:MC:difference}
\end{align}
Thus, the first summand in~\eqref{eq:Gaussian:b:MC:difference} requires a second moment bound for the gradient estimator and an exponential moment bound for the function estimator. The second summand in~\eqref{eq:Gaussian:b:MC:difference} and the error in~\eqref{eq:Gaussian:sigma:MC:difference} require only exponential moment bounds for the function estimator. We derive these bounds in that order. For the gradient estimator, the Gaussian integration by parts identity and $\mathbb E_{g_N,k}[\hat\xi_{i,k}]=0$ give
\begin{align}
\mathbb E_{g_N,k}\left[\widetilde{\nabla} U_{\mu,k}(x)\right]
&=\nabla f(x)+\frac{1}{\mu N}\sum_{i=1}^N
\mathbb E_{g_N,k}\left[
\hat\xi_{i,k}\left(g\left(x+\mu\hat\xi_{i,k}\right)-g(x)\right)\right]\nonumber\\
&=\nabla f(x)+\nabla g_\mu(x)=\nabla U_\mu(x).
\end{align}
Independence within the simulation therefore gives
\begin{align}
\mathbb E_{g_N,k}\left\|\widetilde{\nabla} U_{\mu,k}(x)-\nabla U_\mu(x)\right\|^2
&\leq\frac1N\mathbb E_{g_N,k}\left\|
\frac{\hat\xi_{1,k}}{\mu}
\left(g\left(x+\mu\hat\xi_{1,k}\right)-g(x)\right)\right\|^2\nonumber\\
&\leq\frac{K^2}{N}\mathbb E_{g_N,k}\|\hat\xi_{1,k}\|^4
=\frac{K^2d(d+2)}{N}.
\label{eq:Gaussian:gradient:MC:bound}
\end{align}
Here the variance of the average of $N$ independent centered vectors is $1/N$ times the variance of one vector. The Lipschitz bound $|g(x+\mu\hat\xi)-g(x)|\leq K\mu\|\hat\xi\|$ and the Gaussian moment $\mathbb E\|\hat\xi\|^4=d(d+2)$ give the remaining steps. For the function estimator, define
$$
    F_x(z_1,\ldots,z_N):=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N g(x+\mu z_i).
$$
For $z=(z_1,\ldots,z_N)$ and $z'=(z_1',\ldots,z_N')$ in $\mathbb R^{dN}$,
$$
    |F_x(z)-F_x(z')|
    \leq\frac{K\mu}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N\|z_i-z_i'\|
    \leq\frac{K\mu}{\sqrt N}
    \left[\sum_{i=1}^N\|z_i-z_i'\|^2\right]^{1/2}.
$$
Thus, $F_x$ is $K\mu/\sqrt N$ Lipschitz on $\mathbb R^{dN}$. Since $(\xi_{1,k},\ldots,\xi_{N,k})$ is standard Gaussian in $\mathbb R^{dN}$ and
$$
    \tilde U_{\mu,k}(x)-U_\mu(x)
    =F_x(\xi_{1,k},\ldots,\xi_{N,k}) -\mathbb E_{p_N,k}\left[F_x(\xi_{1,k},\ldots,\xi_{N,k})\right],
$$
the Gaussian concentration inequality gives
\begin{equation}
\mathbb E_{p_N,k}\left[\exp\!\left(\lambda
\bigl(\tilde U_{\mu,k}(x)-U_\mu(x)\bigr)\right)\right]
\leq\exp\!\left(\frac{\lambda^2K^2\mu^2}{2N}\right),
\qquad \forall\lambda\in\mathbb R.
\label{eq:Gaussian:potential:mgf}
\end{equation}
Unbiasedness of the Monte Carlo simulation and Jensen's inequality give, for every $a>0$,
\begin{equation}
\mathbb E_{p_N,k}\left[
e^{-a(\tilde U_{\mu,k}(x)-U_\mu(x))}\right]\geq1.
\label{eq:Gaussian:potential:Jensen}
\end{equation}
Combining \eqref{eq:Gaussian:potential:mgf} with $\lambda=-2$ and \eqref{eq:Gaussian:potential:Jensen} gives
\begin{align}
\mathbb E_{p_N,k}\left |e^{-(\tilde U_{\mu,k}(x)-U_\mu(x))}-1\right |^2
&=\mathbb E_{p_N,k}\left[e^{-2(\tilde U_{\mu,k}(x)-U_\mu(x))}\right]
-2\mathbb E_{p_N,k}\left[e^{-(\tilde U_{\mu,k}(x)-U_\mu(x))}\right]+1\nonumber\\
&\leq e^{2K^2\mu^2/N}-1,
\label{eq:Gaussian:potential:exp:error}
\end{align}
Returning to the expectation of the drift error \eqref{eq:Gaussian:b:MC:difference}, the unbiasedness of the Monte Carlo gradient estimator makes the cross term vanish after taking $\mathbb E_{g_N,k}$. Taking $\mathbb E_{p_N,k}$ then gives
\begin{align}
& \mathbb E_{p_N,k}\mathbb E_{g_N,k}
\left\|\tilde b_k(x)-b(x)\right\|^2
\nonumber\\
&\qquad=e^{2h_\mu(x)}
\mathbb E_{g_N,k}
\left\|\widetilde{\nabla} U_{\mu,k}(x)-\nabla U_\mu(x)\right\|^2
\mathbb E_{p_N,k}\left[e^{-2(\tilde U_{\mu,k}(x)-U_\mu(x))}\right]\nonumber\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad+\left\|\nabla U_\mu(x)\right\|^2e^{2h_\mu(x)}
\mathbb E_{p_N,k}
\left[\left(e^{-(\tilde U_{\mu,k}(x)-U_\mu(x))}-1\right)^2\right]
\nonumber\\
&\qquad\leq \frac{K^2d(d+2)}{N}
e^{2K\mu\sqrt d+2K^2\mu^2/N}\nonumber\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad+\left(\|\nabla f(0)\|+L_fR+K\right)^2
e^{2K\mu\sqrt d}\left(e^{2K^2\mu^2/N}-1\right)
=:A_{\mu,N}.
\end{align}
Here in the inequality, the first term uses \eqref{eq:Gaussian:hmu:sup}, \eqref{eq:Gaussian:gradient:MC:bound} and \eqref{eq:Gaussian:potential:mgf} with $\lambda=-2$. The second term uses \eqref{eq:Gaussian:Gmu:explicit}, \eqref{eq:Gaussian:potential:exp:error}, and \eqref{eq:Gaussian:hmu:sup}. For the diffusion error in \eqref{eq:Gaussian:sigma:MC:difference}, \eqref{eq:Gaussian:potential:mgf} with $\lambda=-1$ and \eqref{eq:Gaussian:potential:Jensen} with $a=1/2$ give
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_{p_N,k}
\left[\left(e^{-(\tilde U_{\mu,k}(x)-U_\mu(x))/2}-1\right)^2\right]
&=\mathbb E_{p_N,k}\left[ e^{-(\tilde U_{\mu,k}(x)-U_\mu(x))}\right] -2\mathbb E_{p_N,k}
\left[e^{-(\tilde U_{\mu,k}(x)-U_\mu(x))/2}\right]+1\\
&\leq e^{K^2\mu^2/(2N)}-1.
\end{aligned}
$$
Combining this estimate with \eqref{eq:Gaussian:hmu:sup} yields
\begin{align}
\mathbb E_{p_N,k}\left[|\tilde\sigma_k(x)-\sigma(x)|^2\right]
&=e^{h_\mu(x)}
\mathbb E_{p_N,k}
\left[\left(e^{-(\tilde U_{\mu,k}(x)-U_\mu(x))/2}-1\right)^2\right]
\nonumber\\
&\leq e^{K\mu\sqrt d}
\left(e^{K^2\mu^2/(2N)}-1\right)
=B_{\mu,N}.
\end{align}
Since $\tilde x_k$ is independent of all the Monte Carlo samples at iteration $k$, iterated expectation gives
\begin{align}
\mathbb E\left\|\tilde b_k(\tilde x_k)-b(\tilde x_k)\right\|^2
&=\mathbb E\left[
\left.\mathbb E_{p_N,k}\mathbb E_{g_N,k}
\|\tilde b_k(x)-b(x)\|^2\right |{x=\tilde x_k}\right]
\leq A_{\mu,N},\nonumber\\
\mathbb E\left|\tilde\sigma_k(\tilde x_k)-\sigma(\tilde x_k)\right|^2
&=\mathbb E\left[
\left.\mathbb E_{p_N,k}|\tilde\sigma_k(x)-\sigma(x)|^2
\right |{x=\tilde x_k}\right]
\leq B_{\mu,N}.
\label{eq:Gaussian:MC:random:bounds}
\end{align}
Substituting~\eqref{eq:Gaussian:ideal:Euler:contraction}, \eqref{eq:Gaussian:ideal:sigma:difference}, and \eqref{eq:Gaussian:MC:random:bounds} into \eqref{eq:Gaussian:coupling:first} closes the one step update:
\begin{align}
\mathbb E\|\tilde x_{k+1}-x_{k+1}\|^2
&\leq\left[(1+\eta)\left(1-2m_\mu\eta+M_\mu^2\eta^2\right)
+4\alpha_\mu\eta\right]\mathbb E\|\tilde x_k-x_k\|^2\nonumber\\
&\qquad\qquad+\eta\left((1+\eta)A_{\mu,N}+4dB_{\mu,N}\right).
\label{eq:Gaussian:coupling:recursion}
\end{align}

We finally solve the resulting recursion. Under \eqref{eq:Gaussian:eta:conservative}, the multiplicative coefficient above satisfies
\begin{align}
&(1+\eta)(1-2m_\mu\eta+M_\mu^2\eta^2)
+4\alpha_\mu\eta
\nonumber
\\
&\qquad=1-\left(2m_\mu-1-4\alpha_\mu\right)\eta
+(M_\mu^2-2m_\mu)\eta^2+M_\mu^2\eta^3\nonumber\\
&\qquad\leq1-(2m_\mu-1-4\alpha_\mu)\eta
+\left(\max\left\{0,M_\mu^2-2m_\mu\right\}+M_\mu^2\right)\eta^2\nonumber\\
&\qquad\leq1-\frac{2m_\mu-1-4\alpha_\mu}{2}\eta.
\end{align}
Since $m_\mu\leq M_\mu$,
\begin{equation}
1-2m_\mu\eta+M_\mu^2\eta^2
=(1-m_\mu\eta)^2+(M_\mu^2-m_\mu^2)\eta^2\geq0.
\end{equation}
We have $1-(2m_\mu-1-4\alpha_\mu)\eta/2$ lies in $[0,1)$. Starting from $\tilde x_0=x_0$, iterate~\eqref{eq:Gaussian:coupling:recursion} to obtain
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E\|\tilde x_k-x_k\|^2
&\leq\eta\bigl((1+\eta)A_{\mu,N}+4dB_{\mu,N}\bigr)\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\left(1-\frac{2m_\mu-1-4\alpha_\mu}{2}\eta\right)^j\\
&=\frac{2\bigl((1+\eta)A_{\mu,N}+4dB_{\mu,N}\bigr)}{2m_\mu-1-4\alpha_\mu}\left[1-\left(1-\frac{2m_\mu-1-4\alpha_\mu}{2}\eta\right)^k\right]\\
&\leq\frac{2\bigl((1+\eta)A_{\mu,N}+4dB_{\mu,N}\bigr)}{2m_\mu-1-4\alpha_\mu}.
\end{aligned}
$$
For $k=0$, the same final bound holds because the error is zero. Finally, the synchronous construction above is itself a coupling of $\nu_k=\mathrm{Law}(x_k)$ and $\tilde\nu_k=\mathrm{Law}(\tilde x_k)$. Hence,
$$
\mathcal W_2^2(\nu_k,\tilde\nu_k)
\leq
\mathbb E\|x_k-\tilde x_k\|^2
\leq
\frac{2}{2m_\mu-1-4\alpha_\mu}
\left((1+\eta)A_{\mu,N}+4dB_{\mu,N}\right),
$$
which is exactly \eqref{eq:Gaussian:MC:W2}. The proof is complete.

body_md:
Fix $\mu$ satisfying the hypotheses. By~\eqref{eq:Gaussian:m:M:alpha} and~\eqref{eq:Gaussian:perturbation:small},
$$
2m_\mu-1-4\alpha_\mu=2\left(m_f-\rho-\frac12-\varepsilon_{b,\mu}-2d\varepsilon_{\sigma,\mu}^2\right)>0.
$$
Lemma~\ref{lemma:Gaussian:sufficient:conditions} therefore verifies Assumptions~\ref{asmpt:strongly:convex} and~\ref{asmpt:smooth} for the exact coefficients in~\eqref{eq:Gaussian:exact:coefficients}, with $(m,M,\alpha)=(m_\mu,M_\mu,\alpha_\mu)$. The present theorem supplies the domain regularity, potential regularity, Poincar\'e inequality, and initial law assumptions required for continuous time convergence. In particular, Proposition~\ref{prop:continuous:structure} supplies the transition semigroup and heat kernel properties. The common initial law also satisfies the interior support condition in Theorem~\ref{thm:final}. Finally, \eqref{eq:Gaussian:eta:conservative} implies $0<\eta\leq1$, and $k\eta\geq e$ is assumed. Thus Theorem~\ref{thm:final} applies to the ideal iterates $x_k$.

Now substituting $U_0=U_\mu$ and the constants in~\eqref{eq:Gaussian:Cbar} into~\eqref{eq:thm:final:explicit} gives
$$
\mathcal W_2(\nu_k,\pi)\leq 2^{3/4}R\left(\chi^2(\nu_0\Vert\pi)\right)^{1/4}e^{-\alpha_{0,\mu}k\eta/(2C_P)}+\bar C_{0,\mu}\eta^{1/4}(k\eta)^{1/2}(\log k)^{1/2}.
$$
Here the first term is the continuous time mixing error and the second is the discretization error. For the same initial law and stepsize, Lemma~\ref{lemma:Gaussian:MC:error} applies to the ideal and Monte Carlo iterates. Taking square roots in~\eqref{eq:Gaussian:MC:W2} yields
$$
\mathcal W_2(\tilde\nu_k,\nu_k)\leq\left(\frac{2\bigl((1+\eta)A_{\mu,N}+4dB_{\mu,N}\bigr)}{2m_\mu-1-4\alpha_\mu}\right)^{1/2}.
$$
Consequently, the triangle inequality gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal W_2(\tilde\nu_k,\pi)&\leq\mathcal W_2(\tilde\nu_k,\nu_k)+\mathcal W_2(\nu_k,\pi)\\
&\leq 2^{3/4}R\left(\chi^2(\nu_0\Vert\pi)\right)^{1/4}e^{-\alpha_{0,\mu}k\eta/(2C_P)}+\bar C_{0,\mu}\eta^{1/4}(k\eta)^{1/2}(\log k)^{1/2}\\
&\qquad+\left(\frac{2\bigl((1+\eta)A_{\mu,N}+4dB_{\mu,N}\bigr)}{2m_\mu-1-4\alpha_\mu}\right)^{1/2},
\end{aligned}
$$
which proves~\eqref{eq:Gaussian:final:W2}.

Fix $\varepsilon>0$ and keep $\mu$ fixed. Since $\alpha_{0,\mu}\geq e^{-K\mu\sqrt d}>0$ by~\eqref{eq:Gaussian:Cbar} and the initial $\chi^2$ divergence is finite, choose a finite $T\geq e$ such that
$$
2^{3/4}R\left(\chi^2(\nu_0\Vert\pi)\right)^{1/4}e^{-\alpha_{0,\mu}T/(2C_P)}\leq\frac\varepsilon3.
$$
For each integer $k$, set $\eta=T/k$. With $T$ fixed, the discretization term becomes
\begin{align}\label{discretization:term}
\bar C_{0,\mu}\eta^{1/4}(k\eta)^{1/2}(\log k)^{1/2}=\bar C_{0,\mu}T^{3/4}\left(\frac{(\log k)^2}{k}\right)^{1/4}\rightarrow0.
\end{align}
The upper bound on $\eta$ in~\eqref{eq:Gaussian:eta:conservative} is strictly positive and independent of $k$ and $N$. Since $T/k\to0$, one can choose an integer $k$ large enough that this stepsize condition holds and the discretization term in \eqref{discretization:term} is at most $\varepsilon/3$. This choice preserves $k\eta=T\geq e$.

It remains to choose $N$ with $T,k,\eta$ now fixed. To verify the required decay directly from~\eqref{eq:Gaussian:A} and~\eqref{eq:Gaussian:B}, use $e^t-1=\int_0^t e^s\,ds\leq te^t$ for $t\geq0$. Since $N\geq1$, this gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
&A_{\mu,N}\leq\frac{e^{2K\mu\sqrt d+2K^2\mu^2}}{N}\left[K^2d(d+2)+2K^2\mu^2\left(\|\nabla f(0)\|+L_fR+K\right)^2\right],
\\
&B_{\mu,N}\leq\frac{K^2\mu^2}{2N}e^{K\mu\sqrt d+K^2\mu^2/2}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Thus both quantities are $\mathcal{O}(N^{-1})$ for the fixed model and smoothing level, and the Monte Carlo error is $\mathcal{O}(N^{-1/2})$. Choose an integer $N$ large enough that
$$
(1+\eta)A_{\mu,N}+4dB_{\mu,N}\leq\frac{\varepsilon^2}{18}\left(2m_\mu-1-4\alpha_\mu\right).
$$
The square root term in~\eqref{eq:Gaussian:final:W2} is then at most $\varepsilon/3$. Each of the three errors is at most $\varepsilon/3$, so their sum is at most $\varepsilon$, the proof is complete.

body_md:
We first bound the normalized scaling factor, then the derivatives of the drift and diffusion coefficients in~\eqref{eq:GS:sharp:coefficients}. Since $g_\delta$ is convex and $K$-Lipschitz, Jensen's inequality and $\mathbb E|G|\leq1$ give
$$
-K\mu\leq U_\delta-U_{\delta,\mu}\leq0,
\qquad
e^{-K\mu}\leq a_\delta^{\rm n}(x) =\frac{e^{U_\delta(x)-U_{\delta,\mu}(x)}}{\int_{\mathcal C}e^{U_\delta-U_{\delta,\mu}}\,d\pi_\delta}
\leq e^{K\mu}.
$$
The quadratic parts cancel in $U_\delta'-U_{\delta,\mu}'$, so
$$
|U_{\delta,\mu}'|\leq\kappa R+K,\qquad |U_\delta'-U_{\delta,\mu}'|\leq2K,\qquad
\kappa\leq U_{\delta,\mu}''\leq\kappa+K/\mu.
$$
The last bound follows from convexity and Gaussian integration by parts:
$U_{\delta,\mu}''-\kappa=\mu^{-1}\mathbb E[Gg_\delta'(x+\mu G)]$, with $|g_\delta'|\leq K$.

For the drift, differentiating $b_\delta^{\rm n}=-a_\delta^{\rm n}U_{\delta,\mu}'$ gives
$$
(b_\delta^{\rm n})' =-a_\delta^{\rm n}\bigl[U_{\delta,\mu}'' +(U_\delta'-U_{\delta,\mu}')U_{\delta,\mu}'\bigr].
$$
Since~\eqref{eq:GS:sharp:admissibility} implies $\kappa-2K(\kappa R+K)>0$, the preceding bounds yield
\begin{align*}
(b_\delta^{\rm n})'\leq-e^{-K\mu}\bigl[\kappa-2K(\kappa R+K)\bigr],\qquad
|(b_\delta^{\rm n})'|\leq e^{K\mu}\bigl[\kappa+K/\mu+2K(\kappa R+K)\bigr].
\end{align*}
For the diffusion, differentiating $\sigma_\delta^{\rm n}=\sqrt{a_\delta^{\rm n}}$ gives directly
$$
|(\sigma_\delta^{\rm n})'|^2 =\tfrac14a_\delta^{\rm n}|U_\delta'-U_{\delta,\mu}'|^2
\leq e^{K\mu}K^2.
$$
The fundamental theorem of calculus gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
&(b_\delta^{\rm n}(x)-b_\delta^{\rm n}(y))(x-y)=(x-y)^2\int_0^1(b_\delta^{\rm n})'(y+t(x-y))\,dt\leq-e^{-K\mu}[\kappa-2K(\kappa R+K)]|x-y|^2,\\
&|b_\delta^{\rm n}(x)-b_\delta^{\rm n}(y)|\leq|x-y|\int_0^1|(b_\delta^{\rm n})'(y+t(x-y))|\,dt\leq e^{K\mu}[\kappa+K/\mu+2K(\kappa R+K)]|x-y|.
\end{aligned}
$$
Similarly, Cauchy-Schwarz inequality on $[0,1]$ gives
$$
|\sigma_\delta^{\rm n}(x)-\sigma_\delta^{\rm n}(y)|^2\leq|x-y|^2\int_0^1|(\sigma_\delta^{\rm n})'(y+t(x-y))|^2\,dt\leq e^{K\mu}K^2|x-y|^2.
$$
These are exactly the three estimates in~\eqref{eq:GS:sharp:bounds}.

body_md:
Fix $\delta>0$ and $0<\eta<\eta_c$. For deterministic $x,y\in\mathcal C$, use the same $G\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$ to define
$$
\begin{aligned}
X_1^x&=\mathcal P_{\mathcal C}\!\left(x+\eta b_\delta^{\rm n}(x)
+\sqrt{2\eta}\sigma_\delta^{\rm n}(x)G\right),\quad
X_1^y=\mathcal P_{\mathcal C}\!\left(y+\eta b_\delta^{\rm n}(y) +\sqrt{2\eta}\sigma_\delta^{\rm n}(y)G\right).
\end{aligned}
$$
These variables have marginal laws $Q^{\rm R}_{\delta,\eta}(x,\cdot)$ and $Q^{\rm R}_{\delta,\eta}(y,\cdot)$. Since projection onto $\mathcal C$ is nonexpansive, $\mathbb EG=0$, and $\mathbb EG^2=1$,
\begin{align*}
\mathbb E|X_1^x-X_1^y|^2
&\leq\mathbb E\left|x-y+\eta\bigl(b_\delta^{\rm n}(x)-b_\delta^{\rm n}(y)\bigr)
+\sqrt{2\eta}\bigl(\sigma_\delta^{\rm n}(x)-\sigma_\delta^{\rm n}(y)\bigr)G\right|^2\\
&=|x-y|^2+2\eta(x-y)\bigl(b_\delta^{\rm n}(x)-b_\delta^{\rm n}(y)\bigr)\\
&\qquad+\eta^2|b_\delta^{\rm n}(x)-b_\delta^{\rm n}(y)|^2
+2\eta|\sigma_\delta^{\rm n}(x)-\sigma_\delta^{\rm n}(y)|^2.
\end{align*}
The mixed term involving $G$ vanishes because the other factors are deterministic. Substituting the three bounds in~\eqref{eq:GS:sharp:bounds}, in the same order, gives
\begin{align*}
\mathbb E|X_1^x-X_1^y|^2
&\leq\Bigl\{1-2\eta e^{-K\mu}\bigl[\kappa-2K(\kappa R+K)\bigr]
+\eta^2M_*^2+2\eta e^{K\mu}K^2\Bigr\}|x-y|^2\\
&=\bigl(1-2\gamma_*\eta+M_*^2\eta^2\bigr)|x-y|^2
=q_\eta^2|x-y|^2,
\end{align*}
where the equality uses the definition of $\gamma_*$ in~\eqref{eq:GS:sharp:constants}. That definition and~\eqref{eq:GS:sharp:admissibility} imply $0<\gamma_*<e^{-K\mu}\kappa<M_*$. Therefore
$$
q_\eta^2 =(1-\gamma_*\eta)^2+(M_*^2-\gamma_*^2)\eta^2>0,
\qquad
q_\eta^2=1-\eta(2\gamma_*-M_*^2\eta)<1,
$$
the last inequality following from $0<\eta<2\gamma_*/M_*^2$.

Now let $(X_0,Y_0)$ be an optimal coupling of $\nu$ and $\nu'$, so that $\mathbb E|X_0-Y_0|^2=\mathcal W_2^2(\nu,\nu')$. Take $G$ independent of this pair and apply the two updates above with $x=X_0$ and $y=Y_0$. The resulting $(X_1,Y_1)$ is a coupling of $\nu Q^{\rm R}_{\delta,\eta}$ and $\nu'Q^{\rm R}_{\delta,\eta}$. Conditioning on $(X_0,Y_0)$ and then taking expectation yields
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal W_2^2\left(\nu Q^{\rm R}_{\delta,\eta},\nu'Q^{\rm R}_{\delta,\eta}\right)
&\leq\mathbb E|X_1-Y_1|^2\leq q_\eta^2\mathbb E|X_0-Y_0|^2 =q_\eta^2\mathcal W_2^2(\nu,\nu').
\end{aligned}
$$
Taking square roots proves~\eqref{eq:GS:sharp:contraction}.

Finally, $\mathcal P_2(\mathcal C)$ is complete in $\mathcal W_2$, and compactness of $\mathcal C$ ensures that every probability measure on $\mathcal C$ has finite second moment. The map $\nu\mapsto\nu Q^{\rm R}_{\delta,\eta}$ sends this space into itself and is a strict contraction with factor $q_\eta<1$. The Banach fixed point theorem therefore gives a unique fixed point $\pi^{\rm R}_{\delta,\eta}$, that is,
$\pi^{\rm R}_{\delta,\eta}Q^{\rm R}_{\delta,\eta}=\pi^{\rm R}_{\delta,\eta}$.
Using this invariance and writing $\nu_{k+1}=\nu_kQ^{\rm R}_{\delta,\eta}$, the one step estimate gives
$$
\mathcal W_2\left(\nu_{k+1},\pi^{\rm R}_{\delta,\eta}\right)
\leq q_\eta\mathcal W_2\left(\nu_k,\pi^{\rm R}_{\delta,\eta}\right).
$$
Induction proves the stated $k$-step bound. Since $\gamma_*$ and $M_*$ depend only on $\kappa,K,R,\mu$, both $\eta_c$ and $q_\eta$ are independent of $\delta$.

title: Proof
body_md:
The RALMC assertion follows from~\eqref{eq:GS:sharp:contraction}, since the first condition in~\eqref{eq:GS:sharp:separation:condition} places $\eta$ in the interval~\eqref{eq:GS:sharp:eta}. We prove the PLMC assertions by computing the response of the projected transition mean to a change in the initial point.

Fix $\delta,\eta>0$ and define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:GS:sharp:projected:mean}
F_\delta(x):=x-\eta U_\delta'(x),\qquad
m_\delta(x):=\int_{\mathcal C}z\,Q^{\rm P}_{\delta,\eta}(x,dz)
=\mathbb E\left[\mathcal P_{\mathcal C}\left(F_\delta(x)+\sqrt{2\eta}G\right)\right].
\end{equation}
The last equality follows from~\eqref{eq:GS:sharp:kernels}. For the potential in~\eqref{eq:GS:sharp:family},
$$
U_\delta'(x)=\kappa x+\frac{Kx}{\sqrt{x^2+\delta^2}},\qquad U_\delta''(x)=\kappa+\frac{K\delta^2}{(x^2+\delta^2)^{3/2}}.
$$
Hence $F_\delta(0)=0$ and $F_\delta'(0)=1-\eta(\kappa+K/\delta)$. Projection onto $[-R,R]$ is the clipping map $\mathcal P_{\mathcal C}(z)=\min\{R,\max\{-R,z\}\}$, whose derivative is $\mathbf1_{(-R,R)}(z)$ away from $z=\pm R$. Since $\sqrt{2\eta}G$ has a continuous density, these two exceptional points have probability zero. Thus, almost surely,
$$
\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\mathcal P_{\mathcal C}(F_\delta(x)+\sqrt{2\eta}G)
-\mathcal P_{\mathcal C}(\sqrt{2\eta}G)}{x} =F_\delta'(0)\mathbf1_{\{|\sqrt{2\eta}G|<R\}}.
$$
To pass this limit through the expectation in~\eqref{eq:GS:sharp:projected:mean}, choose $0<\varepsilon<R$. Nonexpansiveness of projection and the mean value theorem bound the absolute difference quotient by
$$
\frac{|F_\delta(x)-F_\delta(0)|}{|x|}
\leq\sup_{|u|\leq\varepsilon}\left|F_\delta'(u)\right|<\infty,
\qquad 0<|x|\leq\varepsilon.
$$
This deterministic bound is integrable for the fixed $\delta,\eta$. Dominated convergence therefore yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:GS:sharp:mean:derivative}
m_\delta'(0)=F_\delta'(0)\mathbb P\left(\left|\sqrt{2\eta}G\right|<R\right)
=\left[1-\eta\left(\kappa+\frac K\delta\right)\right]p_\eta.
\end{equation}

Then for any coupling $(Y,Z)$ of two probability measures $\rho,\rho'$ with finite second moments, Jensen's inequality gives $|\mathbb EY-\mathbb EZ|^2\leq\mathbb E|Y-Z|^2$. Taking the infimum over couplings yields
$$
\mathcal W_2(\rho,\rho')\geq\left|\int z\,\rho(dz)-\int z\,\rho'(dz)\right|.
$$
Apply this inequality to $Q^{\rm P}_{\delta,\eta}(x,\cdot)$ and $Q^{\rm P}_{\delta,\eta}(0,\cdot)$, whose means are defined in~\eqref{eq:GS:sharp:projected:mean}. Dividing by $|x|$ and using~\eqref{eq:GS:sharp:mean:derivative} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:GS:sharp:mean:W2:lower}
\liminf_{\substack{x\to0\\x\neq0}}
\frac{\mathcal W_2(Q^{\rm P}_{\delta,\eta}(x,\cdot),Q^{\rm P}_{\delta,\eta}(0,\cdot))}{|x|}
\geq\lim_{x\to0}\frac{|m_\delta(x)-m_\delta(0)|}{|x|}=|1-\eta(\kappa+K/\delta)|p_\eta.
\end{equation}
Under~\eqref{eq:GS:sharp:separation:condition}, $\eta(\kappa+K/\delta)>1+p_\eta^{-1}>1$. The absolute value in~\eqref{eq:GS:sharp:mean:W2:lower} is consequently $\eta(\kappa+K/\delta)-1$, and its product with $p_\eta$ is strictly greater than one. This proves~\eqref{eq:GS:sharp:PL:expansion}.

Fix any $\eta\in(0,\eta_c)$, with $\eta_c$ given by~\eqref{eq:GS:sharp:eta}. Since $R,\eta>0$, one has $p_\eta>0$, so the upper bound in~\eqref{eq:GS:sharp:delta:range} is positive. For every $\delta$ in that range,
$$
\eta(\kappa+K/\delta)>\eta K/\delta>1+p_\eta^{-1}.
$$
Thus both conditions in~\eqref{eq:GS:sharp:separation:condition} hold. Finally, if PLMC is globally nonexpansive, then the numerator in~\eqref{eq:GS:sharp:mean:W2:lower} is at most $|x|$ for every $x\in\mathcal C$. Therefore, 
$
|1-\eta(\kappa+K/\delta)|p_\eta\leq1$ gives $
\eta(\kappa+K/\delta)\leq1+p_\eta^{-1}$. For $0<\eta\leq\eta_{\max}$,
$$
p_\eta=\mathbb P\!\left(|G|<\frac R{\sqrt{2\eta}}\right)
\geq\mathbb P\!\left(|G|<\frac R{\sqrt{2\eta_{\max}}}\right)
=p_{\eta_{\max}}>0.
$$
Combining these inequalities proves~\eqref{eq:GS:sharp:PL:necessary}. In particular,
$$
\eta\leq\frac{1+p_{\eta_{\max}}^{-1}}{\kappa+K/\delta}
\leq\frac{1+p_{\eta_{\max}}^{-1}}{K}\,\delta,
$$
which establishes the claimed $O(\delta)$ restriction with a constant independent of $\delta$.

body_md:
We first compute the logarithmic crossing rate for a Gaussian proposal
$$
Y_\eta=x+\eta b+\sqrt{2\eta a}\,G,
$$
where $x\in B$, $a>0$, and $b\in\mathbb R^d$ are fixed as $\eta\to0$. Its density is
$$
p_\eta(y)=(4\pi\eta a)^{-d/2}
\exp\left[-\frac{\|y-x-\eta b\|^2}{4\eta a}\right].
$$
For every $y\in D_+$, the triangle inequality gives
$\|y-x-\eta b\|\geq r_x-\eta\|b\|$. For sufficiently small $\eta$, this lower bound is positive. Since $D_+\subset\mathcal C$,
$$
\mathbb P(Y_\eta\in D_+)
\leq |\mathcal C|(4\pi\eta a)^{-d/2}
\exp\left[-\frac{(r_x-\eta\|b\|)^2}{4\eta a}\right].
$$
Taking logarithms and multiplying by $\eta$, the volume and Gaussian normalization terms tend to zero because $\eta\log\eta\to0$. Hence
$$
\limsup_{\eta\to0}\eta\log\mathbb P(Y_\eta\in D_+)
\leq-\frac{r_x^2}{4a}.
$$
Fix $\varepsilon>0$. By the definition of distance, choose $y_\varepsilon\in D_+$ with $\|y_\varepsilon-x\|<r_x+\varepsilon$. Openness of $D_+$ provides a radius $0<s_\varepsilon<\varepsilon$ such that the ball $\mathcal{B}(y_\varepsilon,s_\varepsilon)$ lies in $D_+$. For every point $y$ of this ball,
$$
\|y-x-\eta b\|
\leq\|y-y_\varepsilon\|+\|y_\varepsilon-x\|+\eta\|b\|
<r_x+2\varepsilon+\eta\|b\|.
$$
Integrating the density over this ball therefore yields
$$
\mathbb P(Y_\eta\in D_+)
\geq |\mathcal{B}(y_\varepsilon,s_\varepsilon)|(4\pi\eta a)^{-d/2}
\exp\left[-\frac{(r_x+2\varepsilon+\eta\|b\|)^2}{4\eta a}\right].
$$
For fixed $\varepsilon$, the ball has positive volume independent of $\eta$. Taking $\liminf$ after multiplying the logarithm by $\eta$ gives
$$
\liminf_{\eta\to0}\eta\log\mathbb P(Y_\eta\in D_+)
\geq-\frac{(r_x+2\varepsilon)^2}{4a}.
$$
Now let $\varepsilon\rightarrow0$ and combine the two bounds to obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:proof:bottleneck:gaussian:ldp}
\lim_{\eta\to0}\eta\log\mathbb P(Y_\eta\in D_+)
=-\frac{r_x^2}{4a}.
\end{equation}
For normalized RALMC, take $a=a_{\rm n}(x)$ and $b=-a_{\rm n}(x)\nabla U_0(x)$ in Equation~\eqref{eq:proof:bottleneck:gaussian:ldp}. For PLMC, take $a=1$ and $b=-\nabla U(x)$. The projection identities at the start of the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:bottleneck:minorization} then give Equation~\eqref{eq:bottleneck:exact:rates}. Subtracting the two limits gives Equation~\eqref{eq:bottleneck:probability:ratio}. Since $r_x>0$, its right hand side is strictly positive if and only if $a_{\rm n}(x)>1$. The final uniform bound follows from $r_x\geq r$ and $a_{\rm n}(x)\geq\rho$.
